{"content": "# Version numbers written with a "post" part are refused

## What happens now

Version numbers that carry a post part, which is the part after a released
version, are turned away with an error. That happens for the short spelling
without a separator, for the spelling with a dot or a dash in front of the
part, and for the spelling with capital letters. Requirements go through the
same check, so a requirement that names such a version is also refused with an
invalid specifier error. One spelling is accepted, the one with a dot and a
number, but the number and the wording of the version are not kept: reading
that version and printing it again gives a different, shorter string, and a
post part of zero disappears from the printed form.

## What should happen

I should be able to read any of the usual ways of writing a post part — with
nothing in front of it, with a dot, with a dash, in lower case or in capital
letters, and with or without a number — and have them all mean the same
version. When I print that version, I should get the same wording back so a
version survives a round trip. A requirement that names such a version should
be accepted too, so I can check whether an installed package matches it.

## About this project

This project is a helper library for Python. It reads version numbers written
as text, sorts them, tells which one is older, and checks a version against a
simple rule such as "at least this version" or "exactly this version". It is
the piece that tools rely on to decide whether two versions match and which
one is newer.

## Problem this solves

Real packages out there are published with post parts written in several
different ways, and people type them the way they have seen them. Right now
those versions cannot be read at all, so anything that has to sort them or
match a version against a rule fails on versions that are perfectly clear to a
person. The one spelling that does work also comes back in a different form
than it went in, which breaks anything that compares the text.

## What changed

Post parts can now be written with no separator, with a dot, or with a dash,
and in capital letters, with or without a number, and all of those forms mean
the same version. A missing number in a post part now counts as zero, the same
way a missing number in the earlier release-candidate and preview parts already
does. The text of a version is now returned the same way it was written, so a
version with a post part keeps its shape. Requirements naming such a version
are accepted. Nothing that worked before stops working: the old spellings and
the plain numeric versions still read and still sort the same way.

## Impact

Compatibility and ease of use. Versions written in common real-world ways
become usable, and the text of a version stays stable when it is read and
written again.

## User experience

Before: I type a version with a post part written with a dash, or in capital
letters, or with nothing in front of the part, and I get an error instead of a
version. And the one spelling that works, with a dot, comes back with a
different number and different wording, so the version I print is not the
version I typed.

After: all of those spellings are read as the post part of that version, and
each one prints back in the same wording I gave. A rule such as "exactly this
version" naming a post part is accepted, so matching works instead of failing
with an invalid specifier error.

- `/workspace/tests/test_version.py`

{"content": "# Post-release version numbers are refused unless written in one exact way

## What happens now
If I write a post-release version with no separator before the word post, such as `1.0post`, or with a dash, such as `1.0-post`, or with a dot and no number, such as `1.0.post`, the library tells me the version is invalid. Only the dotted form with a number, like `1.0.post1`, is accepted. The same spelling rules apply when I write a version requirement, so a requirement written as `==1.0post` is also refused as invalid.

## What should happen
I should be able to write a post-release version in any of the common ways: with no separator before post, with a dot, or with a dash, and with or without a number after the word. The same spelling should work inside a version requirement. When no number is written, the version should be read as post number zero.

## About this project
This is a small library that reads version numbers and version requirements written as text, and compares them so you can tell which is newer. Tools that install software or check dependencies use it to turn strings such as `2.1` or `>=1.0` into something they can compare and match.

## Problem this solves
I cannot compare, sort, or check dependencies against post-release versions written the way people actually write them. A single missing dot or dash makes my whole install or my version check fail even though the meaning is obvious.

## What changed
Post-release versions now accept an optional separator before the word post and an optional number after it, exactly the way development releases already behave. Requirements written with those spellings are accepted too, and a post-release with no number is treated as number zero. Nothing that works today stops working: the dotted form with a number is still read the same way, and the order between pre-releases, plain versions, and post-releases stays the same.

## Impact
Compatibility and ease of use: more real-world version strings are accepted, and fewer installs or version checks fail on a spelling detail.

## User experience
Before: I write `1.0post` and get an invalid version error, and the same thing happens with `==1.0post` in a requirement. After: I write `1.0post` or `1.0-post1` and it is read as a post-release, and a requirement written the same way matches correctly.

## Hints
- /workspace/packaging/version.py
- /workspace/tests/test_version.py

{"content": "# Post releases written without a dot, or without a number, are rejected

## What happens now

If a version ends with a post release, the word post has to be written with a
dot in front of it and a number after it. A version where the word post is
joined straight onto the release numbers, or where it is preceded by a dash,
or where no number follows the word, is turned down with an "Invalid version"
error. The same rule applies when the post release appears inside a
requirement, so a rule that mentions such a post release is refused as well.

## What should happen

Every spelling people actually use for a post release should be accepted: the
word post attached to the numbers, the word post after a dot, the word post
after a dash, the word in capitals, and the word with no number after it at
all. When the number is left out, it should count as zero, and the version
should be shown back in the standard form with the dot and the number filled
in. Rules that mention a post release should accept the same spellings.

## About this project

This project is a small library for working with version numbers. It reads a
version that you give it, tells you whether the version is valid, sorts
versions, and checks a version against a requirement such as a minimum or an
exact match.

## Problem this solves

A lot of projects name their post releases without a dot before the word post,
with a dash instead, or with no number at all. Right now those real releases
cannot be read at all, so a project that uses such a name cannot be installed,
listed, or compared with others.

## What changed

Post releases are read in all the usual spellings instead of only the one
spelling with a dot and a number. A post release with no number is treated as
having a number of zero, and it is printed back with the dot and the number
added. Requirements that mention a post release accept the same spellings.
How versions are ordered against each other, and every other part of the
version such as the pre-release, the development part and the local part,
behave exactly as before. Nothing was taken away.

## Impact

This is about compatibility and ease of use: version names that people
already use stop being rejected, and nothing that worked before changes.

## User experience

Before: I ask the library about a post release where the word post is joined
straight to the numbers, or written after a dash, and I get an "Invalid
version" error even though that name is used by a real project. After: the
same name is accepted, and when I print the version back I get the standard
form with the dot and, where the number was missing, a zero.

## Hints

- /workspace/packaging/version.py
- /workspace/tests/test_version.py
- /workspace/README.rst

## Problem this solves

A lot of projects name their post releases without a dot before the word post,
with a dash instead, or with no number at all. Right now those real releases
cannot be read at all, so a project that uses such a name cannot be installed,
listed, or compared with others.

## What changed

Post releases are read in all the usual spellings instead of only the one
spelling with a dot and a number. A post release with no number is treated as
having a number of zero, and it is printed back with the dot and the number
added. Requirements that mention a post release accept the same spellings.
How versions are ordered against each other, and every other part of a version
such as the pre-release part, the development part and the local part, behave
exactly as before. Nothing was taken away.

## Impact

This is about compatibility and ease of use: version names that people
already use stop being rejected, and nothing that worked before changes.

## User experience

Before: I ask the library about a post release where the word post is joined
straight to the numbers, or written after a dash, and I get an "Invalid
version" error even though that name is used by a real project. After: the
same name is accepted, and when I print the version back I get the standard
form with the dot and, where the number was missing, a zero.

- /workspace/tests/test_version.py
